reaction.title: Hear the snap
todo: Tap the trail to start. Sound on, if you can. The trail also flashes gold.
The moment you hear the SNAP, tap as fast as you can. Try it 3 times.
reaction.tooSoon: You tapped before the snap, so nothing in the world had told you to move yet. Wait for the sound.
reaction.win: Most grown-ups react to a sound in about two-tenths of a second. Kids are often a little slower, and that’s normal. Now the warm-up question: what happened inside you between the snap and your tap? List it in the boxes below.

relay.afterText: All four steps can happen in less than one second.
relay.title: Put the four steps in order
todo: Drag each step onto a station, or tap a step and then tap a station.
Start where the message starts: out in the world.
Fill all four stations and watch the signal run.

why.t: A signal is a tiny message that travels through the body, from a sense organ to the brain, one step at a time.

miss.0: The stimulus is out in the world, like a splash. Nothing happens inside the animal until it does. Try an earlier station.
miss.1: A sense organ can only pick something up after it happens, and it has to pick it up before the brain can decide.
miss.2: The brain decides, but only after a signal reaches it. And the body acts after the brain decides.
miss.3: The response is what the animal does. It’s the very last thing to happen.

relay.win: Signal delivered! Now try the four steps on the SNAP from your warm-up in the Stop & Think below.

cams.title: Open last night’s four cameras
todo: Tap a camera to open it.
Press Next step to follow the message one step at a time.
As you go, ask: what started this animal’s reaction?

why.t: Scientists can’t watch animals all night, so they set up cameras that turn on when something moves.

animals.name: Sea turtle hatchling
steps: Bright moonlight shining on the ocean at night.
Tells the legs to crawl toward the brightest light.
The tiny turtle crawls from its sandy nest toward the ocean.
animals.fact: This is why beach lights can confuse hatchlings. They crawl toward streetlights instead of the sea.
animals.alt: A sea turtle hatchling crawling across wet sand toward the waves, in night-vision green.

animals.name: Florida panther
steps: Sharp ears that can swivel to find where a sound is coming from.
Decides the rustle could be food and tells the legs to freeze, then sneak closer.
The panther moves silently toward the sound.
animals.alt: A Florida panther and two spotted kittens walking past palmettos at night, caught by a trail camera.

animals.name: Manatee
steps: The vibration of a boat motor in the water.
Tiny hairs on its face and body that pick up water movement.
The manatee dives or swims away.
animals.fact: Manatees can’t always notice boats in time. That’s why boat-speed laws matter where manatees live.
animals.alt: A Florida manatee swimming toward the camera underwater, with small fish below it.

animals.name: Cottonmouth
animals.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 110 90"><path d="M10,70 Q30,40 50,62 T84,40" stroke="#B9E3A6" stroke-width="9" fill="none" stroke-linecap="round"/><path d="M80,34 Q96,30 98,38 Q96,46 82,44z" fill="#B9E3A6"/><path d="M98,38 l8,-3 m-8,3 l8,3" stroke="#E8636B" stroke-width="1.6"/><circle cx="90" cy="36" r="1.4" fill="#1B3322"/></svg>
steps: The scent of a frog hiding in the grass at the water’s edge.
Its tongue flicks out to catch tiny bits of smell from the air. A special spot in the roof of its mouth reads them.
The snake glides across the water toward the frog.

sort.subject: Great blue heron
sort.title: Sort the heron’s moment
todo: Read the heron story just above.
Drag each card into its step, or tap a card and then tap a step.
The brain step happens inside the heron, where no camera can see.

why.t: Herons stand very still in shallow water, watch, then strike fast. That makes every step easy to spot, except one.

bins.write: Hidden inside the heron. No camera can film this step.

cards.t: A small fish swims into view.
cards.miss: This happens out in the water before the heron does anything. Which step starts everything?
This is a body part that picks something up. Which step is a body part?

cards.t: It freezes, then strikes and grabs the fish with its beak.
cards.miss: Freezing and striking are things the heron does. Which step is about doing?

sort.win: Sorted! That’s Clue 4. The brain step happened inside the heron, the one step no camera can film.

q1.A: Brain first? The brain can’t decide anything until a message reaches it. What has to happen out in the world before that?
q1.B: A sense organ can’t pick anything up until something happens. Which step is the ‘something happens’?

q2.A: The response is what the panther does, like twisting its ear. The rustling is what it noticed.
q2.C: The sense organ is a body part: the ear. The rustling is out in the world.

q3.B: The stimulus comes from the world, like a splash. The brain is inside the animal.
q3.C: Picking up information is the sense organ’s job: eyes, ears, nose, tongue or skin.

case.title: The Night Everything Moved
case.hook: Last night, four of my trail cameras along the same stretch of Southwest Florida coast caught something strange. In about two minutes, baby sea turtles started crawling, a panther froze, a manatee dove, and a cottonmouth glided away across the water. The cameras were far apart, so the animals couldn’t see or hear each other. Did one big thing set them all off? Or was something else going on?
case.question: What made four animals react at almost the same time, and how did each one know?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

stills.alt: A sea turtle hatchling crawling across wet sand toward the waves, in night-vision green.
A Florida panther and two spotted kittens walking past palmettos at night, caught by a trail camera.
A Florida manatee swimming toward the camera underwater, with small fish below it.

clues.t: A body can react in less than half a second, before you even decide to move. Something happens inside you, fast.
Every reaction runs the same four steps: stimulus → sense organ → brain → response. So each animal must have had its own stimulus.

clues.where: The Lesson: check last night’s four cameras
clues.t: The four cameras show four different stimuli, picked up by four different senses.

clues.where: The Lesson: the heron on CAM 5
clues.t: The heron shows the step no camera can film: inside the animal, the brain decides what the signal means. Then the body moves.

solve.title: What happened that night?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: One loud noise scared all four animals at the same time.
options.why: Check Clue 3. Did all four cameras show the same stimulus? A turtle hatchling crawling toward moonlight isn’t running from a noise.

options.t: Each animal noticed a different stimulus with a different sense, and its own brain decided what to do.
options.why: Case cracked! It looked like one big event, but it was four separate pathways that happened in the same two minutes. Now write your case report: it’s the questions below.
Check the case file: the cameras were far apart, so the animals couldn’t see or hear each other. And Clue 3 shows what each one noticed.

welcome.label: Welcome · the case file
welcome.notes: Optional: you as lead scientist, reading the case file aloud with the four camera stills on screen.
welcome.script: Hi, I’m Dr. Lena Reyes. I study animals in the wild, and last night my trail cameras caught something I can’t explain yet. Four animals, four places, all reacting within about two minutes. I’ve opened a case file, and I need a field scientist to help me solve it. Read the case, then start gathering clues.

warmup.label: Warm-Up
warmup.notes: Do the snap test yourself on camera; show your time.
warmup.script: Before we look at my cameras, let’s look at you. Your body can do something very fast without you planning it. Try the snap test, and pay attention to what happens between the sound and your tap. That’s our first clue.

vocab.label: Word Wall
vocab.notes: Say each word and act it out (snap = stimulus, point to ear, tap head, turn).

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.notes: Walk the four steps with the alligator picture.

part1.label: Part 1 · the four steps
part1.script: Here’s what I know about every animal reaction I’ve ever filmed. Something always starts it, and the animal always does something at the end. The middle is where the mystery hides. So we name every step, and nothing gets to hide from us.

part3.label: Four Florida senses · the cameras
part3.script: These are the four cameras from last night. Open each one and follow what happened, step by step. Here’s what to watch for: what started each reaction? When you’ve seen all four, look at what you found. Does it tell you anything?

explore.label: The heron · CAM 5
explore.notes: Model sorting one heron card (never the brain step).
explore.script: One more camera. This one caught a heron right after the others, and it shows the whole moment from start to finish. Well, almost. One step happens where no camera can see. Sort what the camera caught, and you’ll have your last clue.

assignment.label: Assignment · crack the case
assignment.notes: What each part asks; show the planner and the hint button.
assignment.script: You have the clues. Before you write, decide: what really happened that night? Then write it up like a real field report. Name the steps, use the step words, and back up what you say with what you found.

closing.label: Case closed
closing.script: Case closed. You figured out something it took me a while to see. Next time, we’ll put two very different animals side by side and build models of their pathways. Same four steps. Let’s see what that shows us.

photos.kicker: Look closer · a real Florida manatee
photos.title: What does a manatee use to feel the water?
todo: Tap each number on the photo to read what it is.
Then match the steps to the labels below.

why.t: A real manatee, photographed by U.S. Geological Survey scientists at Crystal River, Florida. It’s the same kind of animal as CAM 3.

photos.alt: A Florida manatee underwater, seen from the side, with whiskers around its mouth and a small eye.
photos.credit: Florida manatee, Crystal River NWR, Florida. U.S. Geological Survey (2015), via Wikimedia Commons

hotspots.label: Whiskers around the mouth
hotspots.t: These stiff whiskers sense touch. Manatees use them to feel plants and other things, a bit like using your fingers.

hotspots.label: A small eye
hotspots.t: Manatees can see, but in cloudy river water eyes don’t help much. That’s one reason touch and hearing matter so much to them.

hotspots.label: Thin hairs on the body
hotspots.t: Look closely along the manatee’s back. Thin hairs are spread across its whole body. Each one can feel water moving, like the push of water from a boat.

hotspots.label: Flipper
hotspots.t: Flippers help a manatee steer, turn and dive. When its brain decides there’s danger, this is part of how it moves away.

task.q: Match each of the manatee’s steps to a label on the photo.

items.miss: Which labels are hairs that can feel things? (There are two right answers.)
items.evid: Whiskers and thin hairs on a manatee’s face and body feel the water move (manatee photo, labels 1 and 3).

items.miss: Which label is a body part the manatee moves with?
items.evid: A manatee steers and dives with its flippers (label 4).

task.win: Photo evidence collected! You can cite it in your answers from the 📎 My evidence drawer on the Assignment tab.

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this help me explain how animals notice and respond?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: A Florida panther has sharp hearing for catching the tiny rustle of a deer.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “panther”, “sharp hearing” and “rustle of a deer”. Those words tell who, which sense, and what it notices. Small words like “the” and “of” don’t carry the idea.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.

lensWin: All six words are in focus. You’ll use every one of them today.

tool.name: Trail camera
tool.teaser: The tool that caught our four animals. It has its own sense organ!
tool.done: You found the camera’s parts, predicted its pictures and sorted its four steps. A trail-camera sticker is in your Field Notebook.

why.q: Why a trail camera this week?
why.t: Trail cameras caught every animal in our case. A trail camera works a lot like an animal: something happens, a sensor notices it, a tiny computer decides, and the camera responds by taking a picture.

cam.title: Look inside a trail camera
todo: Tap each number to learn the camera’s parts.
Play “Will it snap?”: guess before each animal walks by.
Sort the camera’s own four steps.

parts.label: Night flash
parts.t: Rows of tiny lights that glow with infrared light. Infrared light is invisible to people and to most animals, so the camera can take pictures in the dark without scaring anything away.

parts.label: Lens
parts.t: The camera’s eye. It lets light in so the camera can take a picture.

parts.label: Motion sensor
parts.t: This bumpy window is the camera’s sense organ. It senses body heat. When something warmer than the ground around it moves past, like a deer, the sensor notices.

parts.label: Computer chip (inside)
parts.t: A tiny computer inside the case is the camera’s brain. When the sensor sends a signal, the chip decides: is something really there? If yes, it tells the camera to take a picture.

parts.label: Memory card
parts.t: Saves every picture with the date and time, down to the second. That is how Dr. Reyes knew all four animals moved within about two minutes!

scenes.q: A deer walks past, close to the camera.
scenes.why: A deer is warm, it is moving and it is close. The sensor notices the moving body heat, and the chip says “take a picture!”

scenes.q: Wind shakes the palmetto leaves in front of the camera.
scenes.why: Leaves move, but at night they are about as cool as the air. There is no warm body, so the sensor has nothing to notice.

scenes.q: A raccoon waddles past, looking for food.
scenes.why: A raccoon is warm and moving, so the sensor notices its body heat. Snap!

scenes.q: A bobcat crosses the trail far, far away.
scenes.why: It is warm and moving, but too far away. A trail camera’s sensor can only notice animals within a certain distance, usually less than the length of a basketball court.

scenes.q: A snake slides past on a cool night.
scenes.why: Snakes are cold-blooded, so their bodies are about as cool as the ground. The sensor often can’t tell they are there! That is why Dr. Reyes sets her water cameras, CAM 3 and CAM 4, to take a picture every minute, no matter what.

cam.playWin: Nice predicting! A trail camera notices body heat that moves, close by.
